title: Graphs
scopeHtml: Scope: graph representation, DFS and BFS, shortest paths, topological sort, union-find, Dijkstra.

notes.title: Graph representation
notes.html:
Idea. A graph is nodes (vertices) connected by edges, which may be directed or undirected, weighted or unweighted. Most interview graphs are hidden: a grid, a word list, course prerequisites, a social network.

Two common representations.

  • Adjacency list: for each node a list of neighbours. Space O(V + E); best for sparse graphs (almost always the right choice).
  • Adjacency matrix: a V×V table. Space O(V²); O(1) edge check; good only for dense graphs or small V.
Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
// n nodes, edges as pairs (u, v), undirected
vector<vector<int>> buildGraph(int n, vector<vector<int>>& edges) {
    vector<vector<int>> g(n);
    for (auto& e : edges) { g[e[0]].push_back(e[1]); g[e[1]].push_back(e[0]); }
    return g;
}
List<List<Integer>> buildGraph(int n, int[][] edges) {
    List<List<Integer>> g = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) g.add(new ArrayList<>());
    for (int[] e : edges) { g.get(e[0]).add(e[1]); g.get(e[1]).add(e[0]); }
    return g;
}
fun buildGraph(n: Int, edges: Array<IntArray>): List<MutableList<Int>> {
    val g = List(n) { mutableListOf<Int>() }
    for ((u, v) in edges) { g[u].add(v); g[v].add(u) }
    return g
}
from collections import defaultdict

def build_graph(n, edges):
    g = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v in edges:
        g[u].append(v)
        g[v].append(u)
    return g

Vocabulary. Degree (edges at a node), path, cycle, connected component, DAG (directed acyclic graph), bipartite (two-colourable), spanning tree.

Industry examples. Social networks (friends), road maps (weighted), package dependency graphs, web crawling, build systems and recommendation engines.

Everyday analogy. A metro map: stations are nodes and rail segments are edges.

Common interview traps.

  • Forgetting to add both directions for undirected edges.
  • Using a matrix for a sparse graph with 10^5 nodes (10^10 cells).
  • Not handling disconnected graphs: loop over all nodes as starting points.

notes.title: DFS and BFS on grids and graphs
notes.html:
Idea. DFS goes as deep as possible then backtracks (recursion or stack); BFS explores level by level (queue). Both visit each node once: O(V + E). Always mark nodes visited to avoid infinite loops on cycles.

Worked example: Number of Islands on a grid of '1' land and '0' water. Each time you find unvisited land, count one island and flood-fill it.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
void dfs(vector<vector<char>>& g, int r, int c) {
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= (int)g.size() || c >= (int)g[0].size() || g[r][c] != '1') return;
    g[r][c] = '0';                                        // mark visited (sink the land)
    dfs(g, r + 1, c); dfs(g, r - 1, c); dfs(g, r, c + 1); dfs(g, r, c - 1);
}
int numIslands(vector<vector<char>>& g) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < (int)g.size(); r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < (int)g[0].size(); c++)
            if (g[r][c] == '1') { count++; dfs(g, r, c); }
    return count;
}
void dfs(char[][] g, int r, int c) {
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= g.length || c >= g[0].length || g[r][c] != '1') return;
    g[r][c] = '0';                                        // mark visited (sink the land)
    dfs(g, r + 1, c); dfs(g, r - 1, c); dfs(g, r, c + 1); dfs(g, r, c - 1);
}
int numIslands(char[][] g) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < g[0].length; c++)
            if (g[r][c] == '1') { count++; dfs(g, r, c); }
    return count;
}
fun numIslands(g: Array<CharArray>): Int {
    fun dfs(r: Int, c: Int) {
        if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= g.size || c >= g[0].size || g[r][c] != '1') return
        g[r][c] = '0'                                     // mark visited (sink the land)
        dfs(r + 1, c); dfs(r - 1, c); dfs(r, c + 1); dfs(r, c - 1)
    }
    var count = 0
    for (r in g.indices) for (c in g[0].indices) if (g[r][c] == '1') { count++; dfs(r, c) }
    return count
}
def num_islands(g):
    def dfs(r, c):
        if r < 0 or c < 0 or r >= len(g) or c >= len(g[0]) or g[r][c] != "1":
            return
        g[r][c] = "0"                                     # mark visited (sink the land)
        dfs(r + 1, c); dfs(r - 1, c); dfs(r, c + 1); dfs(r, c - 1)

    count = 0
    for r in range(len(g)):
        for c in range(len(g[0])):
            if g[r][c] == "1":
                count += 1
                dfs(r, c)
    return count

Complexity. O(rows × cols) time; recursion depth can reach rows × cols on an all-land grid, so use iterative BFS or increase the stack for big inputs (Python's default recursion limit is about 1000).

DFS or BFS? DFS for exploring all possibilities, components and cycle detection; BFS for the shortest path in an unweighted graph and level-based questions.

Industry examples. Flood fill in image editors, connected-component labelling in vision, web crawlers (BFS from a seed), and "friends of friends within k hops".

Everyday analogy. Spilling paint on a map: it spreads to every connected land cell.

Common interview traps.

  • Not marking visited (infinite recursion) or marking too late (nodes enqueued many times).
  • Recursion depth overflow on large grids.
  • Forgetting diagonal vs 4-direction movement rules.

notes.title: BFS for shortest paths
notes.html:
Idea. In an unweighted graph, BFS reaches every node by the fewest edges first, so the first time you see the target is the shortest path. Track distance per level.

Worked example: Shortest path in a binary matrix (from top-left to bottom-right through 0-cells, 8 directions).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int shortestPathBinaryMatrix(vector<vector<int>>& g) {
    int n = g.size();
    if (g[0][0] || g[n-1][n-1]) return -1;
    queue<array<int,3>> q;                                   // row, col, distance
    q.push({0, 0, 1});
    g[0][0] = 1;                                             // visited
    while (!q.empty()) {
        auto [r, c, d] = q.front(); q.pop();
        if (r == n - 1 && c == n - 1) return d;
        for (int dr = -1; dr <= 1; dr++)
            for (int dc = -1; dc <= 1; dc++) {
                int nr = r + dr, nc = c + dc;
                if (nr >= 0 && nc >= 0 && nr < n && nc < n && g[nr][nc] == 0) {
                    g[nr][nc] = 1;                           // mark when enqueued
                    q.push({nr, nc, d + 1});
                }
            }
    }
    return -1;
}
int shortestPathBinaryMatrix(int[][] g) {
    int n = g.length;
    if (g[0][0] == 1 || g[n-1][n-1] == 1) return -1;
    Deque<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.offer(new int[]{0, 0, 1});                             // row, col, distance
    g[0][0] = 1;                                             // visited
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cur = q.poll();
        int r = cur[0], c = cur[1], d = cur[2];
        if (r == n - 1 && c == n - 1) return d;
        for (int dr = -1; dr <= 1; dr++)
            for (int dc = -1; dc <= 1; dc++) {
                int nr = r + dr, nc = c + dc;
                if (nr >= 0 && nc >= 0 && nr < n && nc < n && g[nr][nc] == 0) {
                    g[nr][nc] = 1;                           // mark when enqueued
                    q.offer(new int[]{nr, nc, d + 1});
                }
            }
    }
    return -1;
}
fun shortestPathBinaryMatrix(g: Array<IntArray>): Int {
    val n = g.size
    if (g[0][0] == 1 || g[n - 1][n - 1] == 1) return -1
    val q = ArrayDeque<IntArray>()
    q.addLast(intArrayOf(0, 0, 1))                           // row, col, distance
    g[0][0] = 1                                              // visited
    while (q.isNotEmpty()) {
        val (r, c, d) = q.removeFirst()
        if (r == n - 1 && c == n - 1) return d
        for (dr in -1..1) for (dc in -1..1) {
            val nr = r + dr
            val nc = c + dc
            if (nr in 0 until n && nc in 0 until n && g[nr][nc] == 0) {
                g[nr][nc] = 1                                // mark when enqueued
                q.addLast(intArrayOf(nr, nc, d + 1))
            }
        }
    }
    return -1
}
from collections import deque

def shortest_path_binary_matrix(g):
    n = len(g)
    if g[0][0] or g[n - 1][n - 1]:
        return -1
    q = deque([(0, 0, 1)])                                   # row, col, distance
    g[0][0] = 1                                              # visited
    while q:
        r, c, d = q.popleft()
        if r == n - 1 and c == n - 1:
            return d
        for dr in (-1, 0, 1):
            for dc in (-1, 0, 1):
                nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and g[nr][nc] == 0:
                    g[nr][nc] = 1                            # mark when enqueued
                    q.append((nr, nc, d + 1))
    return -1

Complexity. O(V + E): each cell is enqueued once. Mark nodes visited when enqueuing, not when dequeuing, otherwise the same node enters the queue many times.

Multi-source BFS. Start with all sources in the queue at distance 0 (rotting oranges, distance to nearest gate). Bidirectional BFS from both ends cuts the search space for word-ladder style problems.

Industry examples. Route finding in unweighted networks, "degrees of separation" in social graphs, minimum moves in game puzzles.

Everyday analogy. A ripple in a pond: the first time it touches a point is the shortest path.

Common interview traps.

  • Using DFS for shortest paths in unweighted graphs.
  • Marking visited on dequeue (exponential blow-up on dense grids).
  • Weighted edges: BFS is wrong; use Dijkstra.

notes.title: Topological sort
notes.html:
Idea. A topological order lists the nodes of a directed acyclic graph so every edge u → v has u before v. It models prerequisites and build orders. If the graph has a cycle, no order exists.

Kahn's algorithm: compute in-degrees, start with all nodes of in-degree 0, repeatedly remove one and decrement its neighbours' in-degrees. If you output fewer than n nodes, there is a cycle.

Worked example: Course Schedule (can all courses be finished given prerequisites?).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool canFinish(int n, vector<vector<int>>& pre) {
    vector<vector<int>> g(n);
    vector<int> indeg(n, 0);
    for (auto& p : pre) { g[p[1]].push_back(p[0]); indeg[p[0]]++; }   // p[1] -> p[0]
    queue<int> q;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.push(i);
    int done = 0;
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front(); q.pop(); done++;
        for (int v : g[u]) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.push(v);
    }
    return done == n;                                                // false means a cycle
}
boolean canFinish(int n, int[][] pre) {
    List<List<Integer>> g = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) g.add(new ArrayList<>());
    int[] indeg = new int[n];
    for (int[] p : pre) { g.get(p[1]).add(p[0]); indeg[p[0]]++; }   // p[1] -> p[0]
    Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.offer(i);
    int done = 0;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int u = q.poll(); done++;
        for (int v : g.get(u)) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.offer(v);
    }
    return done == n;                                                // false means a cycle
}
fun canFinish(n: Int, pre: Array<IntArray>): Boolean {
    val g = List(n) { mutableListOf<Int>() }
    val indeg = IntArray(n)
    for ((course, req) in pre) { g[req].add(course); indeg[course]++ }   // req -> course
    val q = ArrayDeque<Int>()
    for (i in 0 until n) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.addLast(i)
    var done = 0
    while (q.isNotEmpty()) {
        val u = q.removeFirst(); done++
        for (v in g[u]) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.addLast(v)
    }
    return done == n                                                     // false means a cycle
}
from collections import deque

def can_finish(n, pre):
    g = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indeg = [0] * n
    for course, req in pre:
        g[req].append(course)                                # req -> course
        indeg[course] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
    done = 0
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        done += 1
        for v in g[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return done == n                                         # False means a cycle

Complexity. O(V + E). A DFS version uses three colours (unvisited, in-progress, done) and reports a cycle when it meets an in-progress node.

Industry examples. Build systems (Make, Gradle, Bazel), package managers resolving dependencies, task schedulers (Airflow DAGs), spreadsheet cell evaluation order.

Everyday analogy. Getting dressed: socks before shoes, but the order between a shirt and socks does not matter.

Common interview traps.

  • Reversing the edge direction (prerequisite → course).
  • Forgetting that a cycle makes ordering impossible.
  • Disconnected components: enqueue every in-degree-0 node, not just one.

notes.title: Union-Find (disjoint sets)
notes.html:
Idea. Maintain a partition of nodes into groups with two operations: find(x) returns the group's representative and union(a, b) merges two groups. With path compression and union by rank/size each operation is almost O(1) (inverse Ackermann).

Recognise it when: connected components, "are these two nodes connected?", detecting a cycle in an undirected graph, Kruskal's minimum spanning tree, "accounts merge".

Worked example: Number of Connected Components.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
struct DSU {
    vector<int> p, sz; int comps;
    DSU(int n) : p(n), sz(n, 1), comps(n) { iota(p.begin(), p.end(), 0); }
    int find(int x) { return p[x] == x ? x : p[x] = find(p[x]); }       // path compression
    bool unite(int a, int b) {
        a = find(a); b = find(b);
        if (a == b) return false;
        if (sz[a] < sz[b]) swap(a, b);                                   // union by size
        p[b] = a; sz[a] += sz[b]; comps--;
        return true;
    }
};
int countComponents(int n, vector<vector<int>>& edges) {
    DSU d(n);
    for (auto& e : edges) d.unite(e[0], e[1]);
    return d.comps;
}
class DSU {
    int[] p, sz; int comps;
    DSU(int n) { p = new int[n]; sz = new int[n]; comps = n; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { p[i] = i; sz[i] = 1; } }
    int find(int x) { return p[x] == x ? x : (p[x] = find(p[x])); }       // path compression
    boolean union(int a, int b) {
        a = find(a); b = find(b);
        if (a == b) return false;
        if (sz[a] < sz[b]) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }                   // union by size
        p[b] = a; sz[a] += sz[b]; comps--;
        return true;
    }
}
int countComponents(int n, int[][] edges) {
    DSU d = new DSU(n);
    for (int[] e : edges) d.union(e[0], e[1]);
    return d.comps;
}
class DSU(n: Int) {
    private val p = IntArray(n) { it }
    private val sz = IntArray(n) { 1 }
    var comps = n
        private set
    fun find(x: Int): Int { if (p[x] != x) p[x] = find(p[x]); return p[x] }   // path compression
    fun union(a0: Int, b0: Int): Boolean {
        var a = find(a0); var b = find(b0)
        if (a == b) return false
        if (sz[a] < sz[b]) { val t = a; a = b; b = t }                         // union by size
        p[b] = a; sz[a] += sz[b]; comps--
        return true
    }
}
fun countComponents(n: Int, edges: Array<IntArray>): Int {
    val d = DSU(n)
    for ((u, v) in edges) d.union(u, v)
    return d.comps
}
class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.p = list(range(n))
        self.sz = [1] * n
        self.comps = n

    def find(self, x):
        while self.p[x] != x:
            self.p[x] = self.p[self.p[x]]                  # path halving
            x = self.p[x]
        return x

    def union(self, a, b):
        a, b = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if a == b:
            return False
        if self.sz[a] < self.sz[b]:
            a, b = b, a                                    # union by size
        self.p[b] = a
        self.sz[a] += self.sz[b]
        self.comps -= 1
        return True

def count_components(n, edges):
    d = DSU(n)
    for u, v in edges:
        d.union(u, v)
    return d.comps

Complexity. Almost O(1) amortised per operation; O(n + m · α(n)) for m edges.

Industry examples. Network connectivity checks, image segmentation, Kruskal's algorithm for minimum spanning trees (cheapest cable layout), and dynamic connectivity in games.

Everyday analogy. Friend groups merging at a party: when two people meet, their whole groups become one.

Common interview traps.

  • Skipping path compression, which degrades to O(n) per find.
  • Forgetting to call find on both sides before comparing representatives.
  • Using union-find for directed connectivity (it only handles undirected relations).

notes.title: Dijkstra's shortest path
notes.html:
Idea. For graphs with non-negative weights, always settle the closest unsettled node next, using a min-heap keyed by distance. Relax each outgoing edge: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update dist[v] and push it.

Worked example: Network Delay Time (time for a signal from node k to reach every node; return -1 if impossible).

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int networkDelayTime(vector<vector<int>>& times, int n, int k) {
    vector<vector<pair<int,int>>> g(n + 1);                         // node -> (neighbour, weight)
    for (auto& t : times) g[t[0]].push_back({t[1], t[2]});
    vector<int> dist(n + 1, INT_MAX);
    priority_queue<pair<int,int>, vector<pair<int,int>>, greater<>> pq;   // (distance, node)
    dist[k] = 0; pq.push({0, k});
    while (!pq.empty()) {
        auto [d, u] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;                                  // stale entry
        for (auto [v, w] : g[u])
            if (d + w < dist[v]) { dist[v] = d + w; pq.push({dist[v], v}); }
    }
    int ans = *max_element(dist.begin() + 1, dist.end());
    return ans == INT_MAX ? -1 : ans;
}
int networkDelayTime(int[][] times, int n, int k) {
    List<List<int[]>> g = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) g.add(new ArrayList<>());
    for (int[] t : times) g.get(t[0]).add(new int[]{t[1], t[2]});        // (neighbour, weight)
    int[] dist = new int[n + 1];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]); // (distance, node)
    dist[k] = 0; pq.offer(new int[]{0, k});
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cur = pq.poll();
        int d = cur[0], u = cur[1];
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;                                       // stale entry
        for (int[] e : g.get(u))
            if (d + e[1] < dist[e[0]]) { dist[e[0]] = d + e[1]; pq.offer(new int[]{dist[e[0]], e[0]}); }
    }
    int ans = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) ans = Math.max(ans, dist[i]);
    return ans == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : ans;
}
fun networkDelayTime(times: Array<IntArray>, n: Int, k: Int): Int {
    val g = List(n + 1) { mutableListOf<IntArray>() }
    for ((u, v, w) in times) g[u].add(intArrayOf(v, w))                  // (neighbour, weight)
    val dist = IntArray(n + 1) { Int.MAX_VALUE }
    val pq = java.util.PriorityQueue<IntArray>(compareBy { it[0] })       // (distance, node)
    dist[k] = 0; pq.offer(intArrayOf(0, k))
    while (pq.isNotEmpty()) {
        val (d, u) = pq.poll()
        if (d > dist[u]) continue                                        // stale entry
        for ((v, w) in g[u]) if (d + w < dist[v]) { dist[v] = d + w; pq.offer(intArrayOf(dist[v], v)) }
    }
    val ans = (1..n).maxOf { dist[it] }
    return if (ans == Int.MAX_VALUE) -1 else ans
}
import heapq

def network_delay_time(times, n, k):
    g = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for u, v, w in times:
        g[u].append((v, w))                                  # (neighbour, weight)
    dist = [float("inf")] * (n + 1)
    dist[k] = 0
    heap = [(0, k)]                                          # (distance, node)
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue                                         # stale entry
        for v, w in g[u]:
            if d + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = d + w
                heapq.heappush(heap, (dist[v], v))
    ans = max(dist[1:])
    return -1 if ans == float("inf") else ans

Complexity. O((V + E) log V) with a binary heap.

Pick the right algorithm. Unweighted: BFS. Non-negative weights: Dijkstra. Negative weights: Bellman-Ford (O(VE), also detects negative cycles). All pairs on small graphs: Floyd-Warshall (O(V³)). Heuristic search with a goal: A*.

Industry examples. Google Maps and navigation routing (with extensions such as A* and contraction hierarchies), network routing protocols (OSPF), and game AI path planning.

Everyday analogy. Always driving to the nearest unvisited town and updating the best known distance to its neighbours.

Common interview traps.

  • Using Dijkstra with negative edges (incorrect results).
  • Not skipping stale heap entries (d > dist[u]), which can degrade performance.
  • Initialising distance with INT_MAX and then adding weights (overflow).

notes.title: Summary
notes.html: Model the problem as a graph (adjacency list, O(V + E) space) and choose the traversal: DFS for components and exploration, BFS for shortest paths in unweighted graphs and multi-source spreads, always marking visited when enqueuing. Topological sort (Kahn's algorithm) orders a DAG and detects cycles when fewer than n nodes are output. Union-Find with path compression and union by size answers connectivity queries in near-constant time. Dijkstra with a min-heap solves non-negative-weight shortest paths in O((V + E) log V); use Bellman-Ford for negative weights.

questions.promptHtml: When would you use an adjacency list versus an adjacency matrix?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A baseline decision that affects memory and speed.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: An adjacency list takes O(V + E) space and iterates neighbours efficiently, so it is the default for sparse graphs. An adjacency matrix takes O(V²) space but gives O(1) edge checks, which only pays off for dense graphs or small V. A graph with 10^5 nodes would need 10^10 matrix cells.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Most interview inputs come as edge lists; you build an adjacency list in O(E). Remember to add both directions for undirected edges and to loop over all nodes to cover disconnected components.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
vector<vector<int>> buildGraph(int n, vector<vector<int>>& edges) {
    vector<vector<int>> g(n);
    for (auto& e : edges) { g[e[0]].push_back(e[1]); g[e[1]].push_back(e[0]); }
    return g;
}
List<List<Integer>> buildGraph(int n, int[][] edges) {
    List<List<Integer>> g = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) g.add(new ArrayList<>());
    for (int[] e : edges) { g.get(e[0]).add(e[1]); g.get(e[1]).add(e[0]); }
    return g;
}
fun buildGraph(n: Int, edges: Array<IntArray>): List<MutableList<Int>> {
    val g = List(n) { mutableListOf<Int>() }
    for ((u, v) in edges) { g[u].add(v); g[v].add(u) }
    return g
}
from collections import defaultdict

def build_graph(n, edges):
    g = defaultdict(list)
    for u, v in edges:
        g[u].append(v)
        g[v].append(u)
    return g

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:

  2. Implicit graphs (grid, word ladder)? → Generate neighbours on the fly.

questions.promptHtml: Count the islands in a grid. What is the complexity and what could go wrong with recursion?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: The standard connected-components problem on a grid.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Scan every cell; each time you find unvisited land, increment the count and flood-fill the whole island with DFS or BFS, marking cells visited. Time O(rows × cols). Recursive DFS can overflow the stack on large all-land grids, so use BFS or an explicit stack.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Marking visited by overwriting the grid avoids an extra set but mutates the input; copy if that is not allowed. The four-direction versus eight-direction rule must be clarified.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
void dfs(vector<vector<char>>& g, int r, int c) {
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= (int)g.size() || c >= (int)g[0].size() || g[r][c] != '1') return;
    g[r][c] = '0';
    dfs(g, r + 1, c); dfs(g, r - 1, c); dfs(g, r, c + 1); dfs(g, r, c - 1);
}
int numIslands(vector<vector<char>>& g) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < (int)g.size(); r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < (int)g[0].size(); c++)
            if (g[r][c] == '1') { count++; dfs(g, r, c); }
    return count;
}
void dfs(char[][] g, int r, int c) {
    if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= g.length || c >= g[0].length || g[r][c] != '1') return;
    g[r][c] = '0';
    dfs(g, r + 1, c); dfs(g, r - 1, c); dfs(g, r, c + 1); dfs(g, r, c - 1);
}
int numIslands(char[][] g) {
    int count = 0;
    for (int r = 0; r < g.length; r++)
        for (int c = 0; c < g[0].length; c++)
            if (g[r][c] == '1') { count++; dfs(g, r, c); }
    return count;
}
fun numIslands(g: Array<CharArray>): Int {
    fun dfs(r: Int, c: Int) {
        if (r < 0 || c < 0 || r >= g.size || c >= g[0].size || g[r][c] != '1') return
        g[r][c] = '0'
        dfs(r + 1, c); dfs(r - 1, c); dfs(r, c + 1); dfs(r, c - 1)
    }
    var count = 0
    for (r in g.indices) for (c in g[0].indices) if (g[r][c] == '1') { count++; dfs(r, c) }
    return count
}
def num_islands(g):
    def dfs(r, c):
        if r < 0 or c < 0 or r >= len(g) or c >= len(g[0]) or g[r][c] != "1":
            return
        g[r][c] = "0"
        dfs(r + 1, c); dfs(r - 1, c); dfs(r, c + 1); dfs(r, c - 1)

    count = 0
    for r in range(len(g)):
        for c in range(len(g[0])):
            if g[r][c] == "1":
                count += 1
                dfs(r, c)
    return count

  • Python's default recursion limit (~1000) on large grids.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Largest island area? → Return the flood-fill size from DFS.
  2. Islands that arrive over time? → Union-Find with dynamic additions.
  3. Make it iterative? → Explicit stack or queue.

questions.promptHtml: Why does BFS give the shortest path in an unweighted graph, and what is the most common implementation mistake?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Tests the reasoning and a frequent performance bug.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: BFS explores nodes in order of their distance in edges, so the first time it reaches the target is via a shortest path. The common mistake is marking nodes visited when they are dequeued instead of when they are enqueued, which lets the same node enter the queue many times and can blow up the running time.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Track distance by level (queue size per level or storing it with each node). Multi-source BFS starts with several nodes at distance 0, useful for rotting oranges or nearest gate. For weighted graphs BFS is wrong; use Dijkstra.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int shortestPathBinaryMatrix(vector<vector<int>>& g) {
    int n = g.size();
    if (g[0][0] || g[n-1][n-1]) return -1;
    queue<array<int,3>> q;
    q.push({0, 0, 1});
    g[0][0] = 1;
    while (!q.empty()) {
        auto [r, c, d] = q.front(); q.pop();
        if (r == n - 1 && c == n - 1) return d;
        for (int dr = -1; dr <= 1; dr++)
            for (int dc = -1; dc <= 1; dc++) {
                int nr = r + dr, nc = c + dc;
                if (nr >= 0 && nc >= 0 && nr < n && nc < n && g[nr][nc] == 0) {
                    g[nr][nc] = 1;
                    q.push({nr, nc, d + 1});
                }
            }
    }
    return -1;
}
int shortestPathBinaryMatrix(int[][] g) {
    int n = g.length;
    if (g[0][0] == 1 || g[n-1][n-1] == 1) return -1;
    Deque<int[]> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    q.offer(new int[]{0, 0, 1});
    g[0][0] = 1;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cur = q.poll();
        int r = cur[0], c = cur[1], d = cur[2];
        if (r == n - 1 && c == n - 1) return d;
        for (int dr = -1; dr <= 1; dr++)
            for (int dc = -1; dc <= 1; dc++) {
                int nr = r + dr, nc = c + dc;
                if (nr >= 0 && nc >= 0 && nr < n && nc < n && g[nr][nc] == 0) {
                    g[nr][nc] = 1;
                    q.offer(new int[]{nr, nc, d + 1});
                }
            }
    }
    return -1;
}
fun shortestPathBinaryMatrix(g: Array<IntArray>): Int {
    val n = g.size
    if (g[0][0] == 1 || g[n - 1][n - 1] == 1) return -1
    val q = ArrayDeque<IntArray>()
    q.addLast(intArrayOf(0, 0, 1))
    g[0][0] = 1
    while (q.isNotEmpty()) {
        val (r, c, d) = q.removeFirst()
        if (r == n - 1 && c == n - 1) return d
        for (dr in -1..1) for (dc in -1..1) {
            val nr = r + dr
            val nc = c + dc
            if (nr in 0 until n && nc in 0 until n && g[nr][nc] == 0) {
                g[nr][nc] = 1
                q.addLast(intArrayOf(nr, nc, d + 1))
            }
        }
    }
    return -1
}
from collections import deque

def shortest_path_binary_matrix(g):
    n = len(g)
    if g[0][0] or g[n - 1][n - 1]:
        return -1
    q = deque([(0, 0, 1)])
    g[0][0] = 1
    while q:
        r, c, d = q.popleft()
        if r == n - 1 and c == n - 1:
            return d
        for dr in (-1, 0, 1):
            for dc in (-1, 0, 1):
                nr, nc = r + dr, c + dc
                if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and g[nr][nc] == 0:
                    g[nr][nc] = 1
                    q.append((nr, nc, d + 1))
    return -1

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Marking visited on dequeue.
  • Using DFS for shortest paths.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Word Ladder? → BFS over words differing by one letter; bidirectional BFS to speed up.
  2. Weighted edges 0 or 1? → 0-1 BFS with a deque.
  3. Complexity? → O(V + E).

sections.html: Senior knows multi-source and bidirectional variants and 0-1 BFS.

questions.promptHtml: Given course prerequisites, determine whether all courses can be finished. How do you detect a cycle?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Dependency ordering appears in builds, schedulers and package managers.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Build a directed graph from prerequisite to course, compute in-degrees, and run Kahn's algorithm: repeatedly remove nodes with in-degree zero, decrementing their neighbours. If you remove all n nodes the order exists; if fewer, a cycle blocks the rest. O(V + E).

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
A DFS alternative colours nodes unvisited, in-progress and done, and reports a cycle when it meets an in-progress node. The order of removal is a valid topological order, which also answers "return a valid course order".

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
bool canFinish(int n, vector<vector<int>>& pre) {
    vector<vector<int>> g(n);
    vector<int> indeg(n, 0);
    for (auto& p : pre) { g[p[1]].push_back(p[0]); indeg[p[0]]++; }
    queue<int> q;
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.push(i);
    int done = 0;
    while (!q.empty()) {
        int u = q.front(); q.pop(); done++;
        for (int v : g[u]) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.push(v);
    }
    return done == n;
}
boolean canFinish(int n, int[][] pre) {
    List<List<Integer>> g = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) g.add(new ArrayList<>());
    int[] indeg = new int[n];
    for (int[] p : pre) { g.get(p[1]).add(p[0]); indeg[p[0]]++; }
    Deque<Integer> q = new ArrayDeque<>();
    for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.offer(i);
    int done = 0;
    while (!q.isEmpty()) {
        int u = q.poll(); done++;
        for (int v : g.get(u)) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.offer(v);
    }
    return done == n;
}
fun canFinish(n: Int, pre: Array<IntArray>): Boolean {
    val g = List(n) { mutableListOf<Int>() }
    val indeg = IntArray(n)
    for ((course, req) in pre) { g[req].add(course); indeg[course]++ }
    val q = ArrayDeque<Int>()
    for (i in 0 until n) if (indeg[i] == 0) q.addLast(i)
    var done = 0
    while (q.isNotEmpty()) {
        val u = q.removeFirst(); done++
        for (v in g[u]) if (--indeg[v] == 0) q.addLast(v)
    }
    return done == n
}
from collections import deque

def can_finish(n, pre):
    g = [[] for _ in range(n)]
    indeg = [0] * n
    for course, req in pre:
        g[req].append(course)
        indeg[course] += 1
    q = deque(i for i in range(n) if indeg[i] == 0)
    done = 0
    while q:
        u = q.popleft()
        done += 1
        for v in g[u]:
            indeg[v] -= 1
            if indeg[v] == 0:
                q.append(v)
    return done == n

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Reversing the edge direction.
  • Starting from only one zero-in-degree node.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Return an order? → Record nodes as they are dequeued.
  2. Many valid orders? → Any is fine; lexicographically smallest needs a min-heap.
  3. Real-world uses? → Build systems, package managers, Airflow DAGs.

questions.promptHtml: What are path compression and union by size, and why do they make union-find nearly O(1)?

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: A key structure for connectivity problems.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Union-find tracks groups with find (representative) and union (merge). Path compression flattens the tree during find so future finds are shorter, and union by size attaches the smaller tree under the larger so trees stay shallow. Together they give amortised O(α(n)) per operation, effectively constant.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Without these optimisations the structure can degrade into a chain with O(n) finds. It handles undirected connectivity and cycle detection (if find(a) == find(b) before union, the edge forms a cycle), and powers Kruskal's minimum spanning tree.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
struct DSU {
    vector<int> p, sz; int comps;
    DSU(int n) : p(n), sz(n, 1), comps(n) { iota(p.begin(), p.end(), 0); }
    int find(int x) { return p[x] == x ? x : p[x] = find(p[x]); }
    bool unite(int a, int b) {
        a = find(a); b = find(b);
        if (a == b) return false;
        if (sz[a] < sz[b]) swap(a, b);
        p[b] = a; sz[a] += sz[b]; comps--;
        return true;
    }
};
class DSU {
    int[] p, sz; int comps;
    DSU(int n) { p = new int[n]; sz = new int[n]; comps = n; for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { p[i] = i; sz[i] = 1; } }
    int find(int x) { return p[x] == x ? x : (p[x] = find(p[x])); }
    boolean union(int a, int b) {
        a = find(a); b = find(b);
        if (a == b) return false;
        if (sz[a] < sz[b]) { int t = a; a = b; b = t; }
        p[b] = a; sz[a] += sz[b]; comps--;
        return true;
    }
}
class DSU(n: Int) {
    private val p = IntArray(n) { it }
    private val sz = IntArray(n) { 1 }
    var comps = n
        private set
    fun find(x: Int): Int { if (p[x] != x) p[x] = find(p[x]); return p[x] }
    fun union(a0: Int, b0: Int): Boolean {
        var a = find(a0); var b = find(b0)
        if (a == b) return false
        if (sz[a] < sz[b]) { val t = a; a = b; b = t }
        p[b] = a; sz[a] += sz[b]; comps--
        return true
    }
}
class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.p = list(range(n))
        self.sz = [1] * n
        self.comps = n

    def find(self, x):
        while self.p[x] != x:
            self.p[x] = self.p[self.p[x]]
            x = self.p[x]
        return x

    def union(self, a, b):
        a, b = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if a == b:
            return False
        if self.sz[a] < self.sz[b]:
            a, b = b, a
        self.p[b] = a
        self.sz[a] += self.sz[b]
        self.comps -= 1
        return True

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Skipping compression and union by size.
  • Using union-find for directed reachability.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Detect a cycle in an undirected graph? → union returns false for an edge inside a component.
  2. Minimum spanning tree? → Sort edges by weight, union if not already connected (Kruskal).
  3. Accounts merge? → Union emails belonging to the same account.

questions.promptHtml: Explain Dijkstra's algorithm, its complexity, and when it fails.

sections.label: Why interviewers ask this
sections.html: Core shortest-path algorithm with well-known pitfalls.

sections.label: 30-second answer
sections.html: Keep a min-heap of (distance, node). Pop the closest unsettled node, skip stale entries, and relax each neighbour: if dist[u] + w < dist[v], update and push. O((V + E) log V). It fails with negative edge weights, where Bellman-Ford is needed.

sections.label: Deep explanation
sections.html:
Correctness relies on the fact that once the closest node is popped, no later path can be shorter because all weights are non-negative. Lazy deletion (the stale check) avoids needing a decrease-key operation. Use 64-bit distances if sums can overflow.

Languages: C++ · Java · Kotlin · Python
int networkDelayTime(vector<vector<int>>& times, int n, int k) {
    vector<vector<pair<int,int>>> g(n + 1);
    for (auto& t : times) g[t[0]].push_back({t[1], t[2]});
    vector<int> dist(n + 1, INT_MAX);
    priority_queue<pair<int,int>, vector<pair<int,int>>, greater<>> pq;
    dist[k] = 0; pq.push({0, k});
    while (!pq.empty()) {
        auto [d, u] = pq.top(); pq.pop();
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;
        for (auto [v, w] : g[u])
            if (d + w < dist[v]) { dist[v] = d + w; pq.push({dist[v], v}); }
    }
    int ans = *max_element(dist.begin() + 1, dist.end());
    return ans == INT_MAX ? -1 : ans;
}
int networkDelayTime(int[][] times, int n, int k) {
    List<List<int[]>> g = new ArrayList<>();
    for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) g.add(new ArrayList<>());
    for (int[] t : times) g.get(t[0]).add(new int[]{t[1], t[2]});
    int[] dist = new int[n + 1];
    Arrays.fill(dist, Integer.MAX_VALUE);
    PriorityQueue<int[]> pq = new PriorityQueue<>((a, b) -> a[0] - b[0]);
    dist[k] = 0; pq.offer(new int[]{0, k});
    while (!pq.isEmpty()) {
        int[] cur = pq.poll();
        int d = cur[0], u = cur[1];
        if (d > dist[u]) continue;
        for (int[] e : g.get(u))
            if (d + e[1] < dist[e[0]]) { dist[e[0]] = d + e[1]; pq.offer(new int[]{dist[e[0]], e[0]}); }
    }
    int ans = 0;
    for (int i = 1; i <= n; i++) ans = Math.max(ans, dist[i]);
    return ans == Integer.MAX_VALUE ? -1 : ans;
}
fun networkDelayTime(times: Array<IntArray>, n: Int, k: Int): Int {
    val g = List(n + 1) { mutableListOf<IntArray>() }
    for ((u, v, w) in times) g[u].add(intArrayOf(v, w))
    val dist = IntArray(n + 1) { Int.MAX_VALUE }
    val pq = java.util.PriorityQueue<IntArray>(compareBy { it[0] })
    dist[k] = 0; pq.offer(intArrayOf(0, k))
    while (pq.isNotEmpty()) {
        val (d, u) = pq.poll()
        if (d > dist[u]) continue
        for ((v, w) in g[u]) if (d + w < dist[v]) { dist[v] = d + w; pq.offer(intArrayOf(dist[v], v)) }
    }
    val ans = (1..n).maxOf { dist[it] }
    return if (ans == Int.MAX_VALUE) -1 else ans
}
import heapq

def network_delay_time(times, n, k):
    g = [[] for _ in range(n + 1)]
    for u, v, w in times:
        g[u].append((v, w))
    dist = [float("inf")] * (n + 1)
    dist[k] = 0
    heap = [(0, k)]
    while heap:
        d, u = heapq.heappop(heap)
        if d > dist[u]:
            continue
        for v, w in g[u]:
            if d + w < dist[v]:
                dist[v] = d + w
                heapq.heappush(heap, (dist[v], v))
    ans = max(dist[1:])
    return -1 if ans == float("inf") else ans

sections.label: Common mistakes & traps
sections.html:
• Negative edges.
  • Not skipping stale heap entries.
  • Overflow when adding to INT_MAX.

sections.label: Follow-ups
sections.html:
1. Negative weights? → Bellman-Ford, O(VE), also detects negative cycles.
  2. All pairs? → Floyd-Warshall O(V³) or Dijkstra from each node.
  3. Goal-directed search? → A* with an admissible heuristic.

questions.contextHtml: A monorepo build system computes the build order of 3,000 modules from dependency declarations. After a refactor, builds hang forever on some branches, and CI times out after 6 hours. The build tool reports no error. Engineers suspect a performance problem.
questions.promptHtml: What could cause a hang here, and how do you detect and prevent it?

sections.label: What a weak answer looks like
sections.html: Adds more CI machines or increases the timeout.

sections.label: Strong answer
sections.html:
1. Clarifying questions I'd ask: Does the hang correlate with specific commits? Is the dependency graph generated or hand written? Is the scheduler waiting for a module to be ready?
  2. Immediate mitigation: Cancel and revert the offending refactor; add a hard timeout with a clear message.
  3. Hypotheses, ranked: A dependency cycle introduced by the refactor (A depends on B depends on A) so no module ever becomes ready; a scheduler that never reports the cycle; an unusually large graph.
  4. How I'd verify: Run a topological sort on the graph (Kahn's) and check whether all nodes are output; print the remaining nodes with non-zero in-degree.
  5. Root cause: A cycle makes a valid build order impossible; the scheduler waited for modules that waited for each other.
  6. Fix: Fail fast: run the topological sort before building and report the cycle path (for example with a DFS using in-progress colouring and printing the stack). Break the cycle by extracting shared code into a new module.
  7. Prevention: A CI check that validates the module graph on every PR, ownership rules and visibility restrictions, a limit on dependency depth.
  8. Trade-offs: Strict acyclicity enforcement adds friction when refactoring, but it prevents opaque hangs and makes builds parallelisable.

sections.label: Curveball follow-ups
sections.html:
• Optional dependencies? → Model them as separate edges or conditional resolution.
  • Speed up large graphs? → Compute levels from the topological order and build modules in the same level in parallel.

sections.label: Senior war story
sections.html: Adding a graph validation step that printed the exact cycle replaced multi-hour mystery hangs with a one-line error in seconds.

sections.label: Scoring rubric
sections.html:
• No hire: adds machines or timeouts.
  • Hire: identifies a cycle and uses topological sort to detect it.
  • Strong hire: prints the cycle, adds CI validation, parallelises by level.
